interactions.label: Which feature on spirometry best distinguishes asthma from COPD?

params.question: Which feature on spirometry best distinguishes asthma from COPD?

answers.text: Asthma produces a restrictive pattern while COPD produces an obstructive pattern

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Both asthma and COPD are obstructive diseases with a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio; neither produces a restrictive pattern.

answers.text: Asthma shows significant reversibility after bronchodilator, while COPD shows persistent obstruction that is not fully reversible

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Asthma is defined by variable and reversible obstruction (≥12% and ≥200 mL FEV1 improvement after bronchodilator), while COPD has persistent, not fully reversible obstruction — this is the fundamental classification distinction.

answers.text: COPD reduces FVC but spares FEV1, whereas asthma reduces both

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. In both conditions, FEV1 falls disproportionately to FVC, which is why the FEV1/FVC ratio decreases below 0.70.

answers.text: The FEV1/FVC ratio is reduced only in COPD but remains normal throughout in asthma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. During active obstruction the FEV1/FVC ratio is reduced in both diseases; in asthma the ratio may normalise between attacks, but it is not permanently normal.

overallFeedback.feedback: Both asthma and COPD are obstructive conditions with a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio. The key distinction is that asthma demonstrates significant bronchodilator reversibility (≥12% and ≥200 mL FEV1 rise), while COPD does not fully reverse.

Exactly. The hallmark of asthma is reversible obstruction confirmed by bronchodilator response, while COPD shows persistent airflow limitation — this reversibility contrast is the basis for classifying obstructive airway diseases.

params.question: In patients with chronic CO₂ retention, the stimulus to breathe comes from elevated carbon dioxide levels detected by central chemoreceptors.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Not quite. In chronic CO₂ retention, the central chemoreceptors become desensitised to persistently elevated CO₂. The ventilatory drive shifts to the hypoxic stimulus detected by the carotid bodies in the neck — this is why the safe oxygen target in known retainers is 88–92%, not higher.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well done. In chronic CO₂ retainers, the central chemoreceptors have adapted to persistently high CO₂ levels and no longer drive ventilation effectively. The remaining stimulus comes from low oxygen sensed by the peripheral carotid bodies — which is precisely why uncontrolled high-flow oxygen can suppress their breathing and worsen CO₂ retention.

interactions.label: A 62-year-old woman presents with worsening breathlessness over three years, dai

params.question: A 62-year-old woman presents with worsening breathlessness over three years, daily grey sputum production, and a history of cooking over a biomass stove for 30 years. Her symptoms never fully resolve. Which pattern in the history most strongly suggests COPD rather than asthma?

answers.text: Episodic symptoms with complete resolution between attacks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Episodic symptoms with full recovery between attacks is the hallmark of asthma's variable and reversible obstruction, not COPD.

answers.text: Nocturnal wheeze triggered by dust, cold air, and exercise

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Nocturnal symptoms with identifiable environmental triggers such as dust and cold air are characteristic of asthma, not the progressive decline of COPD.

answers.text: Progressive breathlessness with persistent symptoms that never fully clear

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. COPD presents with relentless progression — breathlessness worsens steadily over years, daily sputum production persists, and symptoms never fully resolve, in contrast to asthma's episodic pattern with symptom-free intervals.

answers.text: Seasonal variation in symptoms with completely symptom-free months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Seasonal variation with symptom-free intervals suggests allergic asthma with environmental triggers, not the progressive and persistent course of COPD.

overallFeedback.feedback: COPD is distinguished from asthma in the history by its relentless progression: breathlessness worsens steadily, daily sputum persists, and symptoms never fully resolve — unlike asthma, where episodes clear completely between attacks.

Exactly. The key history contrast is reversibility versus relentless progression — COPD symptoms never fully clear and worsen year on year, while asthma characteristically has symptom-free intervals between attacks.

interactions.label: A 48-year-old smoker has post-bronchodilator spirometry showing FEV1 at 45% of p

params.question: A 48-year-old smoker has post-bronchodilator spirometry showing FEV1 at 45% of predicted and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.62. What is the GOLD severity stage?

answers.text: GOLD 1 — mild

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. GOLD 1 (mild) requires FEV1 ≥80% of predicted. This patient's FEV1 of 45% is far below that threshold.

answers.text: GOLD 2 — moderate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. GOLD 2 (moderate) applies when FEV1 is 50–79% of predicted. At 45%, this patient falls just below the GOLD 2 range.

answers.text: GOLD 3 — severe

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. GOLD 3 (severe) is defined by FEV1 between 30% and 49% of predicted. With FEV1 at 45% and a post-bronchodilator ratio of 0.62 confirming obstruction, this patient has severe COPD.

answers.text: GOLD 4 — very severe

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. GOLD 4 (very severe) applies when FEV1 is below 30% of predicted. This patient's FEV1 of 45% places them in GOLD 3, not GOLD 4.

overallFeedback.feedback: GOLD stages use FEV1 as a percentage of predicted after confirming obstruction (FEV1/FVC <0.70): ≥80% = GOLD 1 (mild), 50–79% = GOLD 2 (moderate), 30–49% = GOLD 3 (severe), <30% = GOLD 4 (very severe). This patient's 45% falls in GOLD 3.
Correct. GOLD severity uses FEV1 as a percentage of predicted: ≥80% is GOLD 1, 50–79% is GOLD 2, 30–49% is GOLD 3, and below 30% is GOLD 4 — memorise these thresholds for clinical practice.

interactions.label: Under the 2023 GINA guidelines, what is the recommended reliever therapy from St

params.question: Under the 2023 GINA guidelines, what is the recommended reliever therapy from Step 1 of asthma management?

answers.text: Salbutamol alone, used as needed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The 2023 GINA guidelines introduced a paradigm shift: a short-acting beta-2 agonist alone is no longer recommended at any step, because it treats bronchospasm without addressing the underlying airway inflammation.

answers.text: Low-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus formoterol, used as needed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. From Step 1, the preferred reliever is now low-dose ICS-formoterol as needed, so that every rescue dose delivers both a bronchodilator and an anti-inflammatory component, reducing the risk of severe exacerbations.

answers.text: Regular oral montelukast as the sole controller

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Montelukast is an add-on therapy useful in specific situations such as aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease or exercise-induced asthma, not the recommended standalone Step 1 treatment.

answers.text: Ipratropium bromide via metered-dose inhaler as needed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Ipratropium is an anticholinergic used primarily in COPD maintenance and acute asthma nebulisation, not as a first-line asthma reliever under current GINA guidelines.

overallFeedback.feedback: The 2023 GINA guidelines removed SABA-only as a recommended reliever at any step. From Step 1, the preferred reliever is low-dose ICS-formoterol as needed, ensuring every rescue dose also treats airway inflammation.
Exactly. The GINA 2023 paradigm shift ensures every rescue puff includes an anti-inflammatory component, addressing the airway inflammation that drives asthma even in the mildest disease.

interactions.label: A 55-year-old COPD patient tells you he knows smoking is harmful but is not yet

params.question: A 55-year-old COPD patient tells you he knows smoking is harmful but is not yet ready to quit. According to the 5As framework, what is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Prescribe varenicline and set a quit date within two weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Setting a quit date and prescribing pharmacotherapy ('Assist') is appropriate only when the patient is ready to quit. Pushing it prematurely risks disengagement and undermines the therapeutic relationship.

answers.text: Assess his readiness to quit using the Prochaska stages and arrange follow-up within one to two weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. 'Assess' his stage of readiness using the Prochaska model, then 'Arrange' follow-up within one to two weeks. Relapse is the rule, not the exception — maintaining contact with empathy keeps the door open for future attempts.

answers.text: Inform him that further bronchodilator prescriptions will be withheld until he agrees to quit

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Withholding treatment is clinically inappropriate and directly contradicts the non-judgmental approach the 5As framework requires. The lecture emphasises that empathy works better than blame.

answers.text: Advise him to switch from cigarettes to bidi as a harm reduction measure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Bidi produces equal or greater tar and nicotine exposure compared to manufactured cigarettes. The 5As framework specifically includes bidi and smokeless tobacco — 'Ask' covers all forms at every visit.

overallFeedback.feedback: When a patient is not ready to quit, the 5As framework directs you to 'Assess' readiness using the Prochaska stages and 'Arrange' follow-up in one to two weeks, maintaining the relationship with empathy rather than judgement.

Well done. When a patient acknowledges harm but is not yet ready to quit, assessing their stage of change and arranging supportive follow-up is the evidence-based approach — empathy and persistence work far better than pressure.
